# Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks Koushik Sinha _Senior Member, IEEE_, Dibakar Saha, Sai Puppala and Bhabani P. Sinha _Fellow, IEEE_ **Abstract--**We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as _G_=(_V,Et_), where _V_={1,2_,...,n_} is the set of _n_ vertices in the graph, and _Et_ is the set of _M_ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size \(T=M\tau,\tau\) being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in _O(M_2_n_3)-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations. **Index Terms--**Temporal graphs, All-pairs shortest paths, Shortest distance path, Shortest time path, Satellite networks, LEO satellite constellations. ### 1 INTRODUCTION W e are witnessing an era of unprecedented expansion in satellite launches, with ambitious plans for multi- orbit, mega-constellations of satellites in the coming decade, involving thousands of interconnected satellites spanning low earth orbit (LEO), medium earth orbit (MEO), and geostationary orbit (GEO). The future of connectivity is quite literally ascending into orbit, with LEO satellite meg- constellations projected to play a pivotal role in that transformation as inter-satellite links (ISLs) become increasingly central to constellation-wide routing and capacity management [1], [2]. With a significantly lower cost to build and launch compared to MEO and GEO satellites, LEO satellites are an extremely attractive proposition for future networks, especially in the context of 6G non-terrestrial networks (NTNs), as their shorter distances from the surface of the Earth translate to lower latency and higher link bandwidth [1]. As such, the concept of mega-constellations of LEO satellites for networking has gained significant traction in recent times, with major operators and programs advancing large-scale deployments and regulatory authorizations [3], [4], [5], [6]. The potential of such space-based networks extends far beyond just providing networking services -- the ability to host in-orbit computing, thereby transitioning satellites into an _integrated communication and computational fabric_ for offloading computation from terrestrial data centers [7]. In May 2025, China reported the launch of an initial set of satellites toward a space computing constellation for collaborative AI-oriented workloads [8]. Related plans have also been discussed publicly for India and Europe in the context of space-based computing and satellite-network capability roadmaps [9], [10]. Similarly, commercial providers have announced space and satellite cloud/edge offerings and supporting ground-to-space service infrastructure [11], [12], [13]. Considering the vast computational resources circling in orbit across the earth, such an in-orbit distributed or edge computing platform can host a myriad of applications, including disaster response, situational awareness for space traffic management, and onboard AI-based filtering and prioritization for Earth-observation data [7]. A key challenge in harnessing LEO satellite constellations for networking, or in-orbit computing, arises from the inherent temporal dynamics of LEO satellite networks. High-speed orbital motion induces time-varying ISL characteristics that lead to dynamic topology changes as satellites traverse deterministic orbital configurations. This predictability enables forward-looking planning and routing mechanisms that explicitly incorporate time dependence [2], [14]. By leveraging the predictable movement of satellites, the network topology for future time slots can be accurately forecasted, and such satellite networks can be represented naturally as time-evolving (temporal) graphs where edges appear and disappear over time [15], [16]. Such a temporal graph can be derived as an ordered list or a stream of timed events, such as additions or deletions of edges as connectivity becomes feasible or infeasible. While a static graph representation for a highly dynamic network topology scenario as encountered in satellite networks suffers from loss of topology-change information, a temporal graph representation with appropriate time granularity is able to capture the full dynamics of the satellite constellation [15].

### 1.1 Basic Idea

We first illustrate the utility of temporal graphs for various application use-cases, followed by how our proposed _all- pairs shortest path algorithm_ can benefit space-based networking and computing.

Furthermore, we often need to distinguish between the distance from a vertex _p_ to another vertex _q_ in terms of the number of traversed edges and the actual time taken to move from _p_ to _q_. This is because one may have to wait at some intermediate vertex for a long time to get the proper connecting edge of the path from _p_ to _q_. Accordingly, multiple temporal-path objectives are used in modern temporal- graph formulations, including shortest-duration (fastest), earliest-arrival, and shortest-length variants [17], [16], [18].

As in-orbit networking and computing becomes a reality, central to the viability of such an infrastructure is efficient computation of up-to-date knowledge of the temporal graph topology characteristics. Accordingly, the _all-pairs shortest path algorithm_ (APSP) is an attractive candidate that can pre-calculate the shortest path between all pairs of routers. Results of APSP computation can be used to populate routing tables. As noted earlier, a temporal graph induced by satellites in LEO exhibits periodic structure at the orbit timescale; for example, representative LEO orbits such as the ISS complete one revolution in roughly ∼90 minutes, illustrating the short recurrence times that motivate orbit- window precomputation. Thus, by executing a temporal all-pairs shortest path algorithm over snapshots captured over one (or multiple) orbital periods, one can pre-calculate temporal shortest paths between any pair of satellites. The resulting temporal shortest paths or routing tables can then be uploaded to the satellites from the ground stations so that whenever a communication request is generated, the appropriate temporal shortest path can be used for near- instantaneous path determination. Moreover, in the event a satellite fails or an ISL’s properties change significantly, pre- computing all-pair temporal shortest paths for contingency scenarios can allow the network to quickly reroute traffic and avoid significant overhead.

### 1.2 Our Contribution

This paper addresses the computation of the shortest time paths between all pairs of vertices in the temporal graph representation of satellite networks. We present an elegant approach for this purpose which essentially involves the multiplication of specific matrices at the core of our proposed algorithm. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents a brief literature survey. In Section 3, we present the preliminaries and network model. Section 4 presents the methodology. Section 5 describes the proposed algorithm. We conclude with the areas of further exploration of this problem in Section 8.

## 2 RELATED WORK

Recent work has continued to expand the algorithmic toolkit for temporal-path problems beyond classical earliest-arrival formulations. Jin et al. [19] study enumerating temporal _s-t_ paths under multiple constraints using temporal subgraph construction and pruning, highlighting the computational challenges created by time-order constraints and large search spaces. Jain and Sahni [18] provide polynomial-time shortest-path algorithms for _interval temporal graphs_, demonstrating that stronger temporal structure can yield tractable shortest-path computation beyond general contact-sequence models. Parallel and hardware-accelerated temporal-path computation has also advanced. Mithinti et al. [20] propose GPU-based parallel algorithms for the fastest-path-duration problem in temporal graphs, indicating that matrix-/scan- like temporal primitives can be mapped effectively to massively parallel architectures. Complementing this, Yu et al. [21] address the overhead of transforming temporal graphs into DAG-style representations for execution, proposing redundancy-aware GPU transformation that improves end-to-end performance of temporal analytics pipelines. These works collectively motivate designs that (i) preserve temporal feasibility exactly (e.g., run/interval constraints) and (ii) expose regular computation patterns suitable for acceleration. Beyond shortest-path computation, recent theoretical work has revisited _periodicity_ and feasibility constraints that arise naturally in recurring systems. Klobas et al. [16] initiate the temporal-graph realization problem with respect to fastest-path durations, including the periodic setting. Their results reinforce that periodic temporal structure is both practically relevant and algorithmically nontrivial, motivating methods that exploit periodicity without collapsing dynamics into static aggregation. In parallel, broad surveys such as Longa et al. [15] summarize the state of temporal graph learning, emphasizing that temporal edges fundamentally change reachability and path semantics, and that realistic dynamic systems require time-aware modeling choices.

For LEO mega-constellations, multiple recent studies focus on coping with topology dynamics, laser-ISL operational constraints, and scalable planning. Bhattacharjee et al. [22] consider _on-demand_ routing when dynamic laser inter-satellite links incur non-negligible setup delays, presenting optimization and heuristic schemes evaluated on Starlink-like constellations. Ron et al. [14] propose a dynamic time-expanded-graph (DTEG) based approach for time-dependent topology optimization under multi-objective criteria (capacity, latency, churn), reflecting growing interest in explicitly time-dependent design objectives. At a higher planning layer, Cen et al. [2] introduce SatFlow, a scalable framework that jointly plans topology, traffic allocation, and terminal power allocation for mega- constellations, addressing both dynamics and operational cost at scale. Demand-aware topology design has also been explored in very recent work: Dehshali et al. [23] propose a traffic-driven heuristic (Starfield) to orient ISLs toward non- uniform demand patterns, reporting improvements over baseline topologies in packet-level simulation.

Complementing routing and planning, link- configuration and feasibility modeling continues to evolve.<tbc>

<tbc>Ren et al. \[24\] study ISL allocation as a multi-objective optimization problem under dynamic topology and resource limits. At the physical-layer/network interface, Gioulis et al. \[25\] present a constellation-aware optical ISL model that evaluates power requirements across an orbital period, supporting more realistic feasibility constraints for temporal adjacency. Finally, learning-based routing in dynamic LEO settings has also gained traction; Riyad et al. \[26\] report Q-learning based routing over snapshot- derived topologies, reflecting a trend toward adaptive routing under time-varying connectivity.

Taken together, recent literature shows (i) renewed algorithmic attention to temporal shortest/fastest path computation and its acceleration, and (ii) rapidly growing interest in time-dependent routing/planning for LEO mega- constellations with laser ISLs. Our work targets the intersection of these themes by focusing on all-pairs shortest _communication-time_ paths under discrete-time feasibility constraints, with an implementation structure intentionally aligned with parallelizable primitives.

## 3 NETWORK MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS

This section introduces the basic preliminaries of the network model and the assumptions.

### 3.1 Preliminaries

We introduce a model of the temporal graph to be used for our later discussions, which is formulated around the concepts of time-varying connectivity in a temporal graph as given in \[27\], but with some modifications. The following components describe our model:

#### 3.1.1 Temporal graph representation

We denote a temporal graph as _G_=(_V,E<sub>t</sub>_), where \(V=\{1,2,\cdots,n\}\) is the set of _n_ vertices in the graph and _E<sub>t</sub>_ is the set of time-varying edges considered over a time window of size _T_ starting from time _t_=0 to _t=T_. This time window of observation will be represented as _W_=\[0_,T_\].

#### 3.1.2 Time Window

In general, a temporal edge \(e_{pq}\in E_t\) connecting two vertices _p_ and _q_ during this time window _W_ will be represented by a tuple \((p,q,[t_1,\Delta t_1],[t_2,\Delta t_2],\cdots,[t_k,\Delta t_k])\), where the vertices _p_ and _q_ are connected only during the non-overlapping time durations \([t_i,t_i+\Delta t_i],i=1,2,\cdots,k\) with the time ordering of \(0\le t_1<t_1+\Delta t_1<t_2<t_2+\Delta t_2<\cdots<t_k<t_k+\Delta t_k\le T\). An example of such time-varying connections is shown by the horizontal line segments in Fig. 1 for _k_=3. We refer to these time durations \([t_i,t_i+\Delta t_i],i=1,2,\cdots,k\) as the _connectivity durations_ for the vertices _p_ and _q_ during the observation window \[0_,T_\], and denote these by _CD<sub>pq</sub>_\[0_,T_\] or simply _CD<sub>pq</sub>_ when the time window \[0_,T_\] is implied from the context.

#### 3.1.3 Time slots for each snapshot

We divide the time window \[0_,T_\] in equal intervals of time duration \(\tau\) (refer to Fig. 1 for a diagrammatic representation), where a snapshot of the connectivity is taken during each such interval. Each interval’s length \(\tau\) may be set to the<tbc>

<tbc>most petite possible duration used to observe the graph’s time-varying nature with maximum temporal resolution. The exact value of \(\tau\) may be chosen depending on the requirements of typical real-life applications, e.g., phone calls, email communications, etc., for which the temporal graph model will be used.

**Example 1.** _For example, the message transmission delay can be computed as_ \(\mathcal{D}=\frac{\mathcal{Q}_\sharp}{\mathcal{B}}\) _, where Q is the size of the message m and B is the bit rate of a channel in a particular band \[28\]. Therefore, consider a node v<sub>i</sub> starts the transmission of message m of size_ 10_MB at a time slot t over GSM band_ 20_MHz. Then, the communication latency can be computed as:_ \(\mathcal{D}=\frac{10}{20}=0.5\) _seconds. But in case the same message will be sent through GSM Band_ 10_MHz, then_ D _will be_ \(\mathcal{D}=\frac{10}{20}=1\) _seconds. Hence, we consider the value of_ \(\tau\) _depending on the current availability of the channel bandwidth and the size of the message to be sent. In this example,_ \(\tau\) _will be set to one second, and for each second, we take the snapshot accordingly._

We assume that \(T=M\tau\), so that there will be a total of _M_ snapshots, numbered as \(0,1,2,\cdots,M-1\) taken during these _M_ intervals \([0,\tau],[\tau,2\tau],\cdots,\dots[(M-1)\tau,T]\), respectively to provide the total connectivity information of every edge of the temporal graph during the time window \[0_,T_\] under consideration. An interval _I=j_ will refer to the time duration from \(j\tau\) to \((j+1)\tau\).

Two vertices _p_ and _q_ will be connected by an edge _e<sub>pq</sub>_ during the _j<sup>th</sup>_ snapshot, \(j\in\{0,1,2,\cdots,M-1\}\), if there is a continuous connectivity of duration at least \(\lambda\tau\) (\(0<\lambda<1\)) during the interval \([j\tau,(j+1)\tau]\) which also has a non-null intersection with at least one of the _k_ connectivity durations \([t_i,t_i+\Delta t_i],i=1,2,\cdots,k\) of the vertices _p_ and _q_. Note that, \(\lambda\) can be a priori fixed depending on the specific application requirements.

### 3.2 Assumptions

\(\bullet\) We assume that a finite amount of time is needed to traverse every edge in the path, and the snapshot interval \(\tau\) is so small that this time to traverse an edge is always more than \(\tau\). Without loss of generality, we assume for simplicity that this time to traverse an edge can be expressed as some non-zero integral multiple of \(\tau\).

\(\bullet\) During the whole time window \[0_,T_\], the distance _d<sub>pq</sub>_ from _p_ to _q_, as well as the time _t<sub>pq</sub>_ to traverse the edge _e<sub>pq</sub>_ from _p_ to _q_ (when it exists throughout the period _t<sub>pq</sub>_) will be assumed to be constant. Given these information, it may be noted that when we start traversing the edge _e<sub>pq</sub>_ at any time during the interval _I=j_, i.e., during \([j\tau,(j+1)\tau]\), this connecting edge _e<sub>pq</sub>_ must exist continuously during the interval \([j\tau,(j+t_{pq})\tau]\) for the completion of the traversal.

\(\bullet\) A temporal graph will be represented by an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix _A_ whose (_p,q)<sup>th</sup>_ entry will be a 3- tuple given as _A(p,q_)=(_CS<sub>pq</sub>,d<sub>pq</sub>,t<sub>pq</sub>_).

## 4 METHODOLOGY

Consider a temporal path \(p_1p_2\cdots p_m\) from a vertex _p_<sub>1</sub> to another vertex _p<sub>m</sub>_ that exists in the temporal graph _G_=(_V,E<sub>t</sub>_) during the time window _W_=\[0_,T_\] under consideration. After reaching a vertex \(p_j,j=2,3,\cdots,m-1\) along the path from the vertex _p_<sub>_j_-1</sub>, a connection from _p<sub>j</sub>_ to _p_<sub>_j_+1</sub> following the trail should be continuously available (without any break) in any subsequent _t_<sub>_p<sub>j</sub>p_<sub>_j_+1</sub></sub> snapshot intervals. To satisfy this requirement, one may have to wait at the vertex _p<sub>j</sub>_ for some time until the required connectivity to the vertex _p_<sub>_j_+1</sub> is guaranteed. We illustrate this situation by the following example.

**Example 3.** _Consider a temporal graph with five vertices for which the vertex set is V_={1,2,3,4,5}_. The connecting edges are time-varying in nature with the aggregated static graph as shown in Fig. 2 during an observation window_ \([0,10\tau]\)_. One possibility is that we start at interval I_=0 _to reach vertex 4 traversing the edge e_<sub>14</sub> _during the intervals 0 and 1, wait there for two time intervals and then traverse the edge e_<sub>43</sub> _during the intervals 4 and 5. Thus, we reach vertex 3 at interval I_=5 _and the total time of travel is 6 units._

We construct a path matrix _P_ whose (_p,q)<sup>th</sup>_ entry will contain information about all such possible contact periods and will be represented as \((\nu_{pq},(I_s^{pq}[1],I_f^{pq}[1],pred^{pq}[1])\), \((I_s^{pq}[2],I_f^{pq}[2],pred^{pq}[2])\), \(\cdots\) , \((I_s^{pq}[\nu_{pq}],I_f^{pq}[\nu_{pq}],pred^{pq}[\nu_{pq}])\)), where \(\nu_{pq}\) is the number of possible paths from _p_ to _q_, and the 3-tuple \((I_s^{pq}[i],I_f^{pq}[i],pred^{pq}[i])\) contains information about the starting interval, finishing interval and the corresponding predecessor vertex of _q_ in the _i<sup>th</sup>_ path, \(1\le i\le\nu_{pq}\). As special cases, the entries of \(P(p,p),p\in V\) will be set to (0,(0,0,0)) and also when there will be no path from _p_ to _q_, the entries of _P(p,q_) will be set to \((0,(0,0,\infty))\).

With the above idea, the path matrix _P_ is first initialized based on 1-adjacency of the vertices, following the algorithm _initialize\_path\_matrix_ as shown in Procedure 2. After that, to find the all-pairs shortest time paths, we would augment each entry of the path matrix with information about other possible contacts (as expressed through a 3- tuple \((I_s^{pq}[i],I_f^{pq}[i],pred^{pq}[i])\)), if any, through more than one edge. Thus, the (_p,q)<sup>th</sup>_ entry of _P_ will finally contain information about all possible paths from _p_ to _q_ indicated by the \(\nu_{pq}\) 3-tuples \((I_s^{pq}[i],I_f^{pq}[i],pred^{pq}[i])\), \(1\le i\le\nu_{pq}\). Finally, from all these \(\nu_{pq}\) tuples, the one with the minimum value of \((I_f^{pq}[i]-I_s^{pq}[i])\) will be chosen as the path with the shortest time from _p_ to _q_.

To achieve the above objective of computing the final path matrix, we proceed as follows. Assume that we have already computed the contact information for a path from _p_ to _q_ with the corresponding entry in the path matrix _P(p,q_) as \((I_s^{pq}[i],I_f^{pq}[i],pred^{pq}[i])\). Suppose, from the vertex _q_, we would now like to reach another vertex _r_ adjacent to _q_ where _A(q,r_)=(_CS<sub>qr</sub>,d<sub>qr</sub>,t<sub>qr</sub>_). It will be possible to reach the vertex _r_ from _q_ if we find some \(j>I_f^{pq}[i]\) such that there is a run of \(1's\) of length _t<sub>qr</sub>_ in _CS<sub>qr</sub>_ starting from the interval _j_, i.e., \(CS_{qr}[j]=CS_{qr}[j+1]=\cdots=CS_{qr}[j+t_{qr}-1]=1\), for some \(j>I_f^{pq}[i]\). Once such a run is found, the total time of traversal from _p_ to _r_ will be \(j+t_{qr}-I_s^{pq}[i]\). The start time and finish time from _p_ to _r_ through _q_ will also be accordingly evaluated as \(I_s^{pq}[i]\) and _j+t<sub>qr</sub>_-1, respectively and _pred<sup>pr</sup>_\[_i_\] will be set to _q_. The corresponding 3-tuple \((I_s^{pq}[i],j+t_{qr}-1,q)\) will then be inserted as a new 3-tuple in _P(p,r_) in the sorted order of \((I_s^{pr},I_f^{pr})\) values provided there is no other existing 3-tuple with the same values of \((I_s^{pr},I_f^{pr})\), to avoid duplicate entries which might be generated in the above process of finding the possible contacts.

The above operation will be repeated with all the \(\nu_{pq}\) tuples \((I_s^{pq}[i],I_f^{pq}[i],pred^{pq}[i])\), \(1\le i\le\nu_{pq}\). Collectively, we denote all these operations symbolically by \(P(p,q)\otimes A(q,r)\). The algorithm for computing \(P(p,q)\otimes A(q,r)\) is presented in the form of _update\_all\_possible\_contacts(A,P,p,r_) as given in Procedure 3.

With these preliminary ideas, we describe below an algorithm for computing all-pairs shortest time paths as described in the next section.

To compute the all-pairs shortest time paths in a temporal graph, we adopt the basic concept of in-place ordered matrix multiplication in Hu’s algorithm mentioned above and introduce appropriate modifications on it to deal with the time-varying nature of the connecting edges. First, the matrix multiplication is equivalently replaced by an operation where, in computing an element of the product matrix, the multiplication of two elements of a matrix is replaced by \(\otimes\) operation between _P_ and _A_ and second, the summation of these computed products is replaced by augmenting each of the (_p,q)th_ entries, \(1\le p,q\le n\) of the product matrix with the newly generated 3-tuples containing information of additional contacts from _p_ to _q_ during the period under consideration. Finally, from each such (_p,q)th_ entry of the product matrix, the 3-tuple with the minimum time between the start and finish intervals is chosen to find the shortest time path from _p_ to _q_. Our proposed algorithm for computing all-pairs shortest time paths of a temporal graph is shown in Algorithm 1, where we essentially perform the in- place computation of the path matrix \(P(p,r),1\le p,r\le n\) through a forward and backward process of this equivalent matrix multiplication operation. A vertex in a path is said to be a minimum vertex if it is less than its predecessor and successor vertices in the path. A sequence of vertices \(p_1,p_2,\cdots,p_k\) in a path is said to form i) an upward sequence if \(p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_k\), ii) a downward sequence if \(p_1>p_2>\cdots>p_k\), and iii) a valley sequence if there is only one minimum vertex in the sequence and \(min(p_1,p_k)>max_j(p_j),j=2,3,\cdots,k-1\).

We now have the following lemma.

**Lemma 1.** _If the vertices which are in a shortest time path_ \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) _from a vertex p_<sub>1</sub> _to a vertex p<sub>k</sub> form an upward sequence or a downward sequence, then this shortest time path from p_<sub>1</sub> _to p<sub>k</sub> will be computed in the forward process of Algorithm 1._

_Proof._ If the vertices in order as in the path form an upward sequence, then \(p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_k\). Hence, in the forward process, _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>2</sub>) is computed first with the direct edge from _p_<sub>1</sub> to _p_<sub>2</sub> in the initialization phase itself. Next, _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>4</sub>) will assume the final value from the operation \(P^F(p_1,p_3)\otimes P(p_3,p_4)\), and so on to get the order of computation as \(P^F(p_1,p_2)<P^F(p_1,p_3)<P^F(p_1,p_4)<\cdots<P^F(p_1,p_k)\) during the forward process itself. This fact is pictorially represented in Fig. 3(a) where the labels on dotted lines show the steps of computation and the solid lines show the availability of connecting edges during the time window under consideration.

Similarly, if the vertices in the shortest time path \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) form a downward sequence, then \(p_1>p_2>\cdots>p_k\). Thus, _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>_k_-1</sub>_,p<sub>k</sub>_) is computed first with the direct edge from _p_<sub>_k_-1</sub> to _p<sub>k</sub>_, then _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>_k_-2</sub>_,p<sub>k</sub>_) is computed using this value of _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>_k_-1</sub>_,p<sub>k</sub>_) by the operation \(P^F(p_{k-1},p_k)\otimes P(p_{k-2},p_{k-1})\), and so on to get the order of computation as \(P^F(p_{k-1},p_k)<P^F(p_{k-2},p_k)<\cdots<P^F(p_2,p_k)<P^F(p_1,p_k)\) in the forward process itself. Fig. 3(b) pictorially represents this order of computation in the forward process corresponding to the upward sequence \(p_1>p_2>\cdots>p_k\) of vertices in the path.

**Lemma 2.** _If the vertices in a shortest time path_ \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) _from a vertex p_<sub>1</sub> _to a vertex p<sub>k</sub> form a valley sequence, then this shortest time path will be computed in the forward process of Algorithm 1._<tbc>

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _p<sub>j</sub>_ be the minimum of all vertices \(p_1,p_2,\cdots,p_k\) in the valley sequence. Then the sequence from _p_<sub>1</sub> to _p<sub>j</sub>_ will be a downward sequence and that from _p<sub>j</sub>_ to _p<sub>k</sub>_ will be an upward sequence. By Lemma 1, _P<sup>F</sup>(p_<sub>1</sub>_,p<sub>j</sub>_) will be computed in the forward process. Further, we note that during the forward process, \(P^F(p_1,p_j)<P^F(p_1,p_{j+1})<\cdots<P^F(p_1,p_k)\). Hence the proof.

For an arbitrary sequence of vertices in a shortest time path \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) from a vertex _p_<sub>1</sub> to a vertex _p<sub>k</sub>_, if there are multiple valley sequences within the sequence \(p_1,p_2,\cdots,p_k\), then each such valley sequence, say \(p_s,p_{s+1},\cdots,p_t\), the shortest time path from _p<sub>s</sub>_ to _p<sub>t</sub>_ will be computed in the forward process by virtue of Lemma 2. Let us delete all vertices in between _p<sub>s</sub>_ and _p<sub>t</sub>_ (keeping only _p<sub>s</sub>_ and _p<sub>t</sub>_) in the sequence and repeat this step for each such valley sequence in succession. If a new valley sequence is formed after this deletion process, then also the process is repeated to delete all intermediate vertices within such a valley sequence. Note that in every instance of such a valley sequence, the portion of the shortest time path \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) formed with the vertices of the valley sequence will be computed by virtue of Lemma 2. After such deletion process, eventually we will be left out with either i) an upward sequence, or ii) a downward sequence or ii) an upward sequence followed by a downward sequence. If the resulting reduced sequence is an upward or a downward sequence, the shortest time path with these vertices in the reduced sequence will be computed by virtue of Lemma 1. We now have the following lemma.

**Lemma 3.** _If the vertices in a shortest time path_ \(p_1p_2\cdots p_k\) _from p_<sub>1</sub> _to p<sub>k</sub> form an upward sequence followed by a downward sequence, then this shortest time path will be computed by the backward process of Algorithm 1._

_Proof._ Assume that the vertex _p<sub>j</sub>_ is maximum of all vertices \(p_1,p_2,\cdots,p_k\) in the path. Hence, \(p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_j\). From the order of execution of loops in the backward process, we get, \(P^B(p_{j-1},p_j)<P^B(p_{j-2},p_j)<P^B(p_{j-3},p_j)<\cdots<P^B(p_1,p_j)\). Thus the upward section of the shortest time path is computed in the backward process. Likewise, since \(p_j>p_{j+1}>\cdots>p_k\), we get, \(P^B(p_j,p_{j+1})<P^B(p_j,p_{j+2})<\cdots<P^B(p_j,p_k)\), i.e., the downward section of the shortest time path is also computed in the backward process. We further note that the computation order in the backward process leads us to the following result: \(P^B(p_1,p_j)<P^B(p_1,p_{j+1})<P^B(p_1,p_{j+2})<\cdots<P^B(p_1,p_k)\). Hence the proof.

All these discussions lead to the following result :

**Theorem 1.** _Algorithm 1 correctly computes the all-pairs shortest time paths in a temporal graph._

## 6 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

This section describes the experimental design in a way that directly validates the modeling choices and algorithmic primitives introduced in Sections 3 and 4. In particular, we validate: (i) snapshot-based temporal discretization and the construction of connectivity strings _CS<sub>pq</sub>_; (ii) the run-length feasibility constraint of length _t<sub>pq</sub>_ used by Procedure 1; (iii) correctness of the path-matrix updates (Procedure 3) relative to trusted baselines; (iv) the necessity of the forward and backward passes in Algorithm 1; and (v) the computational scaling behavior implied by Theorem 2. We also quantify the network-level implications of optical range constraints and waiting-vs-traversal behavior that are unique to temporal routing.

### 6.1 Experimental Goals and What We Validate

The experiments are organized around four validation questions that map one-to-one to the methodology:

1) **Temporal-graph validity:** Does the snapshot construction produce meaningful time-varying adjacency consistent with LEO geometry, and does the resulting _CS<sub>pq</sub>_ capture periodic contact patterns over one orbit?<tbc>

2) **Run-length feasibility validity:** Do run-length requirements (Procedure 1) correctly enforce the model assumption that a hop (_p,q_) is traversable only when _CS<sub>pq</sub>_ contains a contiguous run of ones of length \(\ge t_{pq}\) after packet arrival?<tbc>

3) **Algorithmic correctness validity:** Does Algorithm 1 compute the same shortest communication-time outcomes as baselines that are known-correct (time- expanded graph shortest paths, and temporal Dijkstra-like methods) on problem sizes where those baselines are feasible?<tbc>

4) **Computational scaling validity:** Do runtime and memory scale with (_n,M_) in a way consistent with Theorem 2, and does the matrix-style update structure admit practical acceleration via data-parallel kernels (bit operations and batched run detection)?<tbc>

<tbc>We report both _algorithmic_ metrics (run- time/memory/scaling and baseline agreement) and _network_ metrics (reachability, shortest communication time, hop count, and waiting fraction).

### 6.2 Observation Window and Snapshot Discretization \((T,M,\tau)\)

As described in the methodology, we represent the network as a temporal graph over an observation window _W_=[0_,T_] divided into _M_ snapshots of duration \(\tau\) such that \(T=M\tau\). For LEO constellations, the topology is strongly periodic due to deterministic orbital dynamics. Therefore, we choose _T_ to span approximately one orbital period, so that the temporal graph contains a full recurrence of link formation and dissolution.

In the main experiments we use a nominal orbital period of _P_<sub>orb</sub>=96 minutes (LEO-like), and perform sensitivity checks for \(P_\mathrm{orb}\in[90,128]\) minutes. For each \(\tau\) we set<tbc>

\(M=\left\lceil\frac{P_\mathrm{orb}}{\tau}\right\rceil,\) (1)

<tbc>and sweep temporal resolution using

\(\tau\in\{5,10,20\}\text{s.}\) (2)

For _P_<sub>orb</sub>=96 minutes this yields _M_={1152,576,288} snapshots.

**Discretization validity check.** To validate that the snapshot durations are fine-grained enough for contact modeling, we measure (i) snapshot-wise average degree over time (Fig. 7), and (ii) link-run statistics derived from _CS<sub>pq</sub>_ ( 6). The goal is to ensure that observed connectivity is not an artifact of overly coarse sampling (missing short contacts) or overly fine sampling (inflating _M_ without changing routing outcomes).

### 6.3 Constellation Mobility and Link Feasibility Model

Satellite positions are computed using deterministic Keplerian orbit propagation. This guarantees that the induced temporal graph is structured and periodic, which is central to our motivation for precomputation over one orbit. At each snapshot index \(j\in\{1,\dots,M\}\), an optical ISL between satellites (_p,q_) is declared feasible if

\(d_{pq}(j)\le R,\) (3)

where _d<sub>pq</sub>(j_) is the inter-satellite distance at snapshot _j_, and _R_ is the optical range threshold. We evaluate

\(R\in\{659,1319,1500,1700\}\text{km.}\) (4)

For each (_p,q_) we construct the connectivity string

\(CS_{pq}^{(R)}[j]=\unknown\{d_{pq}(j)\le R\},\) (5)

which matches the connectivity-string definition in Section 3. This binary string is the primitive consumed by Procedure 1 for finding the next contiguous run of ones.

Because temporal routing depends on _when_ neighbors appear and disappear, we validate the time-varying adjacency behavior using a node-centric storyboard across consecutive snapshots. Figures 4 and 5 show a focus satellite<tbc>

This validates that the topology evolves substantially within one orbit and that static aggregation would be misleading, motivating the temporal model.

## 6.4 Traversal-Time Requirement and Run-Length Feasibility

As assumed in the methodology, traversing an edge is not instantaneous and requires _t<sub>pq</sub>_ snapshot units; therefore, a hop (_p,q_) is admissible only if a contiguous run of ones of length at least _t<sub>pq</sub>_ exists in _CS<sub>pq</sub>_ starting after the packet arrives at _p_. This is exactly the rule enforced by Procedure 1.

In the main results we use a conservative baseline _t<sub>pq</sub>_=2 snapshots for all feasible links, capturing non-propagation effects such as pointing/acquisition, scheduling, buffering, and framing overhead. We also perform sensitivity checks with \(t_{pq}\in\{1,2\}\) to quantify how stricter run requirements affect reachability and waiting.

To validate that run structure is the mechanism that drives waiting, we visualize feasibility timelines using a connectivity-string heatmap for a focus satellite and its neighbors (Fig. 6). We then compute standard run-length features ( 6), including duty cycle, run-length percentiles, and gap-length percentiles. These metrics link directly to Procedure 1: shorter runs and longer gaps increase the frequency with which the algorithm must search forward in time to find the next feasible transmission window.

## 6.5 Algorithmic Evaluation: Correctness, Necessity of Two Passes, and Baselines

For each range threshold _R_, we build the temporal adjacency matrix _A_<sup>(_R_)</sup> whose entries follow the tuple structure in Section 3, and compute the path matrix _P_<sup>(_R_)</sup> using Algorithm 1. Each \(P^{(\tilde{R})}(p,q)\) returns the selected shortest communication-time tuple \((I_s^{pq},I_f^{pq},pred^{pq})\) after Procedure 4.

We validate correctness against two known-correct baselines that optimize the same objective as our method: minimum end-to-end communication time (minimum duration). First, we construct a directed _time-expanded graph_ _G_<sub>TE</sub>=(_V_<sub>TE</sub>_,E_<sub>TE</sub>) whose node set is \(V_\mathrm{TE}=\{(v,t)|v\in V,t\in\{0,1,\dots,M-1\}\}\). To represent waiting and transmission under our run-feasibility constraint, we add (i) _wait edges_ \((v,t)\rightarrow(v,t+1)\) of weight 1 for all \(v\in V\) and _t\<M_-1, and (ii) _traverse edges_ \((p,t)\rightarrow(q,t+t_{pq})\) of weight _t<sub>pq</sub>_ if and only if the hop (_p,q_) is admissible at time _t_, i.e., \(CS_{pq}[t]=CS_{pq}[t+1]=\cdots=CS_{pq}[t+t_{pq}-1]=1\). For each ordered pair (_s,d_), we compute the shortest-path distance in _G_<sub>TE</sub> from (_s,t<sub>s</sub>_) to (_d,t<sub>f</sub>_) and then minimize over all possible departure times _t<sub>s</sub>_, namely \(\mathrm{min}_{t_s\in\{0,\dots,M-1\}}\mathrm{dist}_{G_\mathrm{TE}}\big((s,t_s),(d,\cdot)\big)\). This value equals the minimum number of snapshot intervals spent waiting plus traversing, and therefore equals \(\mathcal{T}_{sd}/\tau\) under the same run-length feasibility rule enforced by Procedure 1; as a result, _G_<sub>TE</sub> provides a known-correct baseline for the exact objective optimized by Algorithm 1.

As a second, independent correctness check, we implement a _temporal Dijkstra-like_ shortest-duration algorithm<tbc>

<tbc>(run for a subset of sources) over the same state space (_v,t_) with the same two transition types: unit-weight waiting transitions and admissible traverse transitions that require a contiguous run of ones of length at least _t<sub>pq</sub>_ beginning at the transmission time. This single-source baseline optimizes the same end-to-end duration objective T_<sub>sd</sub>_ and serves to validate our path-matrix update rules through an algorithmic approach that is structurally different from the time- expanded shortest-path computation.

For each tested pair (_p,q_) we compare: (i) whether a path exists (reachability agreement), (ii) the returned communication time \((I_f-I_s+1)\tau\) (latency agreement), and (iii) the reconstructed hop sequence (path agreement, when computed). We report the fraction of pairs with exact latency match and the maximum absolute latency deviation (in snapshots and seconds).

The methodology motivates performing two ordered sweeps--first forward and then backward--to ensure that optimal paths with different structural vertex-order patterns are discovered. We validate the necessity of this design experimentally by running three algorithm variants: a _forward-only_ version that executes only the forward loops in Algorithm 1, a _backward-only_ version that executes only the backward loops, and the _full_ version that performs both passes (forward+backward) as proposed.

We measure the fraction of pairs for which forward- only (or backward-only) matches the full solution in communication time and reachability. Any mismatch indicates that the omitted pass is necessary for discovering certain optimal path structures, consistent with the proof intuition in Lemmas 1-3.

## 6.6 Scalability Design: Full APSP vs. Pair Sampling at Mega-Constellation Scale

At mega-constellation scale (\(n\approx 2\times 10^4\)), the number of ordered pairs is _n(n_-1), which is too large for exhaustive path extraction and storage in experimental evaluation. Therefore, while we still construct temporal connectivity primitives over all satellites, we evaluate routing statistics using randomized sampling of ordered pairs.

Unless stated otherwise, we sample:

\(\bullet\) _N_<sub>pairs</sub>=50,000 distinct ordered pairs per _R_ for reachability and latency distributions, and<tbc>

\(\bullet\) _N_<sub>pairs</sub>=10,000 per _R_ for hop-count and waiting/traversal decomposition (requires path reconstruction).

We repeat each configuration _K_=5 times with different random seeds and report mean \(\pm\) standard deviation.

## 6.7 Metrics Reported (Directly Tied to Methodology)

We report the following metrics, each of which corresponds directly to quantities defined in Section 4:

\(\bullet\) Reachability ratio: fraction of pairs for which _P(p,q_) contains a valid tuple (not \((0,0,\infty)\)).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Shortest communication time: \(\mathcal{T}_{pq}=(I_f^{pq}-I_s^{pq}+1)\tau\).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Hop count: obtained by following predecessor pointers _pred<sup>pq</sup>_ backward to reconstruct the selected path.

\(\bullet\) Waiting vs traversal: traversal time \(T_\mathrm{trav}=\sum_\mathrm{hops}t_{uv}\tau\) and waiting time _T_<sub>wait</sub>=T_<sub>pq</sub>-T_<sub>trav</sub>, and waiting fraction _f<sub>w</sub>=T_<sub>wait</sub>/T_<sub>pq</sub>_.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Temporal density: snapshot-wise average degree \(\bar{k}_t(R)\) over _t_=1_,...,M_ (Fig. 7) and summary statistics ( 7).

These metrics validate the intended behavior of the model: under intermittent contacts, shortest communication time depends not only on hop count but also on waiting induced by misalignment with feasible runs in _CS<sub>pq</sub>_.

## 7 RESULTS

This section reports results in the same order as the validations defined in Section 6, and in direct correspondence with the methodology in Section 4. Recall that (i) the temporal graph is represented by snapshot-wise edge sets encoded as connectivity strings \(CS_{pq}^{(R)}\), (ii) a hop (_q,r_) is admissible only if there exists a _future_ contiguous run of ones of length \(\ge t_{qr}\) in \(CS_{qr}^{(R)}\) (Procedure 1), and (iii) the algorithm returns for each ordered pair (_p,q_) a shortest communication-time tuple \((I_s^{pq},I_f^{pq},pred^{pq})\) (Algorithm 1) from which the end-to-end time is \(\mathcal{T}_{pq}=(I_f^{pq}-I_s^{pq}+1)\tau\). We first validate the temporal connectivity primitives (including % links found/missing), then validate correctness via baseline comparison, then report performance (run- time/memory/scaling), and finally connect temporal contact structure to waiting-vs-traversal behavior in shortest- time paths.

### 7.1 Methodology-to-Metrics Mapping

For a given range threshold _R_, let \(E_t^{(R)}\) denote the set of feasible inter-satellite links at snapshot _t_:

\(E_t^{(R)}=\{(p,q)|CS_{pq}^{(R)}[t]=1\},t\in\{1,\dots,M\}.\) (6)

This snapshot-based temporal representation is standard in temporal-network modeling \[30\], \[31\]. Algorithm 1 produces a path matrix _P_ whose entry _P(p,q_) stores the selected shortest communication-time contact tuple \((I_s^{pq},I_f^{pq},pred^{pq})\) after Procedure 4. We compute:

\(\bullet\) Shortest communication time: \(\mathcal{T}_{pq}=(I_f^{pq}-I_s^{pq}+1)\tau\).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Hop count _H_: recovered by following predecessor pointers _pred<sup>pq</sup>_ backward.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Traversal time: \(T_\mathrm{trav}=\sum_\mathrm{hops}t_{uv}\tau\).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Waiting time: _T_<sub>wait</sub>=T_<sub>pq</sub>-T_<sub>trav</sub> and waiting fraction _f<sub>w</sub>=T_<sub>wait</sub>/T_<sub>pq</sub>_.

These metrics align exactly with the admissibility and tuple- composition rules in Section 4.

### 7.2 Validation 1: Temporal Connectivity Dynamics and Link Churn (Percentage Found / Percentage Missing)

We first validate that the temporal adjacency varies substantially over time, and quantify _how much_ connectivity changes between consecutive snapshots. Figures 4 and 5 show a focus satellite (S7) and its neighborhood across four consecutive snapshots, visually demonstrating link appearance/disappearance at short timescales. Space-time / snapshot modeling is widely used in satellite-network topology analysis \[33\], \[34\].

4 quantifies neighborhood churn for the focus node via persistent/new/dropped neighbors and Jaccard similarity. High turnover indicates that a packet arriving at an intermediate satellite often encounters a different set of outgoing options than existed one snapshot earlier, increasing the probability of waiting for a future admissible run.

To quantify link volatility at the constellation scale, we define the _found_ (new) and _missing_ (dropped) link sets between consecutive snapshots:

\(E_\mathrm{found}^{(R)}(t)=E_t^{(R)}\backslash E_{t-1}^{(R)},\) (7)

\(E_\mathrm{missing}^{(R)}(t)=E_{t-1}^{(R)}\backslash E_t^{(R)}.\) (8)

We then report the corresponding percentages:

\(\%\mathrm{Found}(t)=100\cdot\frac{|E_\mathrm{found}^{(R)}(t)|}{|E_{t-1}^{(R)}|+\epsilon},\) (9)

\(\%\mathrm{Missing}(t)=100\cdot\frac{|E_\mathrm{missing}^{(R)}(t)|}{|E_{t-1}^{(R)}|+\epsilon},\) (10)

where \(\epsilon\) is a small constant used only to avoid division- by-zero in extremely sparse snapshots. These churn and similarity summaries are commonly used to characterize temporal adjacency dynamics \[30\], \[31\].  5 summarizes these churn percentages over one orbit; as expected, smaller _R_ yields higher churn and therefore more waiting- dominated routing.

### 7.3 Validation 2: Connectivity Strings Capture Contact Runs (Run-Length View)

The algorithm’s admissibility check (Procedure 1) is based on contiguous runs of ones in \(CS_{pq}^{(R)}\). Temporal-path feasibility under time-respecting constraints is a core concept in temporal graphs \[32\], \[30\]. Consequently, if connectivity is fragmented, a packet may arrive during a "0" period or within a run shorter than _tpq_ and must wait until a sufficiently long run appears.

We now connect temporal contact structure to end-to-end routing behavior. For sampled source-destination pairs, we compute shortest communication-time paths and decompose total time into traversal and waiting components:

### 7.8 Discussion and Engineering Implications

The results establish a methodology-consistent chain from physical feasibility to temporal routing performance. The optical feasibility threshold _R_ directly shapes temporal adjacency by controlling snapshot-wise degree and link churn: smaller _R_ produces sparser graphs with higher %Found/%Missing (greater intermittency), whereas larger _R_ increases link persistence and smooths connectivity over time ( 5). These adjacency dynamics translate into the run structure of connectivity strings \(CS_{pq}^{(R)}\), where larger _R_ yields longer runs of ones and shorter gaps ( 6), increasing the likelihood that the run-length admissibility condition (\(\ge t_{uv}\)) is satisfied immediately after packet arrival. As a consequence, improved run persistence reduces buffering and waiting at intermediate nodes, shifting shortest-time routes from waiting-dominated behavior in contact-limited regimes toward traversal-dominated behavior in connectivity-rich regimes (Fig. 8,  10). From an algorithmic standpoint, the high agreement with time- expanded and temporal shortest-path baselines ( 8) supports the correctness of tuple composition in Procedure 3 under the same admissibility rules, while the measured runtime and memory trends ( 9) clarify where full APSP is practical and where sampled-pair evaluation becomes necessary at mega-constellation scale. Collectively, these findings motivate cross-layer co-design: _R_ shapes the temporal contact fabric \(CS_{pq}^{(R)}\), while discretization \(\tau\) and per-hop requirement _t<sub>pq</sub>_ set the feasibility threshold that governs waiting. The joint choice of \((R,\tau,t_{pq})\) therefore determines whether the constellation operates as a low- latency mesh or as a contact-limited delay-tolerant network.
